title: Blue carbon ecosystem accounting
bottleneck: Mangroves, seagrasses, and salt marshes bury carbon efficiently, but quantifying their sequestration is plagued by lateral carbon transport — much of the carbon moves offshore rather than staying buried — and by methane and nitrous oxide emissions from the same wetlands that offset the CO2 benefit. Site-level variability is enormous, and default accounting factors can be wrong by multiples. Restoration projects thus struggle to produce defensible carbon credits.
why_it_blocks: Blue carbon is politically attractive because it pairs climate action with coastal protection and fisheries. Bad accounting means credits may represent little real removal, and over-crediting could displace genuine emissions cuts.
current_state: Methodologies from major registries now include blue carbon, and research is refining lateral-flux corrections and greenhouse-gas budgets. But the science remains site-specific, and scaling credible blue carbon finance is still held back by measurement costs.
